title: Song of Solomon 2:1–7
context: The WEB assigns 2:1 to the Beloved, 2:2 to the Lover, and 2:3–7 to the Beloved. She describes herself modestly as a rose of Sharon and a lily of the valleys (the exact flowers are uncertain); he answers that she is like a lily among thorns; and she compares him to an apple tree among the trees of the wood, under whose shadow she rests with delight. She speaks of being brought to the banquet hall under a banner of love, of being faint with love, and of a secure embrace. The section closes with a refrain addressed to the daughters of Jerusalem, urging them not to stir up or awaken love until it so desires; the refrain returns in 3:5 and, in shorter form, in 8:4. Readers in both Arminian and Reformed traditions commonly take the refrain as counsel to patience and restraint, so that love is not rushed. Literal readers commonly see here the security and delight of committed love, while figurative readers commonly hear the believer’s rest and joy in God or in Christ. Both readings are commonly held within each tradition, and the passage is shared ground.

verses.text: I am a rose of Sharon, a lily of the valleys.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Beloved describing herself as a rose of Sharon and a lily of the valleys, a modest image of simple beauty. Love sees worth in the ordinary.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a humble self-description. Many older readers applied the words to Christ, while others read them as the Beloved’s; readers in both traditions commonly hold either view with care.

verses.text: As a lily among thorns, so is my love among the daughters.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Lover answering that she is like a lily among thorns. Love values the beloved above every other.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the contrast as an image of beauty in the midst of difficulty. Figurative readers commonly hear the church kept lovely in a hard world, a reading found in both traditions.

verses.text: As the apple tree among the trees of the wood, so is my beloved among the sons. I sat down under his shadow with great delight, his fruit was sweet to my taste.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Beloved comparing him to an apple tree among the trees of the wood and resting in his shade with delight. Love brings rest and refreshment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see shelter and satisfaction in the beloved. Figurative readers commonly hear the believer resting in Christ and tasting his goodness (compare Psalm 34:8; Psalm 91:1).

verses.text: He brought me to the banquet hall. His banner over me is love.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Beloved brought to the banquet hall, with love as his banner over her. Love is public, joyful, and protective.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the banner of love as a sign of belonging and security. Figurative readers commonly hear God’s love openly declared over his people, an image both traditions cherish.

verses.text: Strengthen me with raisins, refresh me with apples; for I am faint with love.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Beloved asking for raisins and apples because she is faint with love. Love can overwhelm and calls for gentle care.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the intensity of love honestly described. Figurative readers commonly hear the soul overwhelmed by a sense of God’s love and needing his strengthening.

verses.text: His left hand is under my head. His right hand embraces me.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Beloved speaking of a secure embrace. Literal readers see the comfort and safety of committed love.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see an image of protection and closeness. Figurative readers commonly hear the security of God’s people held by his care, and readers in both traditions treat the line with restraint.

verses.text: I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, or by the hinds of the field, that you not stir up, nor awaken love, until it so desires.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the refrain urging the daughters of Jerusalem not to stir up or awaken love until it so desires. Love is to be guarded and not rushed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see wise counsel to patience and restraint. Readers in both traditions commonly read the refrain as shared ground about waiting for love’s proper time (compare Ecclesiastes 3:1; 1 Corinthians 13:4).
